projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charles Zito was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Now what do you want to know?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Wait. We're interviewing Charles Zito.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: They all call me Charlie Z.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Okay. Start.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: All right. All right. When I was 9 years old, I had polio.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: So I didn't qualify for anything in the service. I had a bad leg. You knew that.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: In 1942, I became a flight instructor, and I still have -- the license is still good, it doesn't expire until 2004.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: So it's right here. Then I became a flight instructor at the Carlisle, you know the law school Carlisle, civilian training detachments, then I went all over, whenever the program ended, I went some other places, then one day the war ended, right.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: They posted me to be a B-29 flight engineer because I was a flight engineer before I went to the Army in Middletown, I was a flight engineer. Then the war ended, right, the European war ended. They posted me to the B-29 flight school, B-29 engineering school in Emerald, Texas, then the war ended, and they said, Charlie, do you want to go home or do you want to go to Army occupation? I had two children at home, Charlie was still here, Chlorinda was here. Charlie in '45 was four years old, Chlorinda was only two years old, right, and Charlie went home, and I have a certificate of service. I've never been discharged from the Army because I was never physically qualified to be in the service. I still have a bad leg, you knew that.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Been in the hospitals a bunch of times, haven't I?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: You saw me in bad condition, haven't you?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: I was there.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I almost died one time.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: They were hoping I would, they'd get my money, but I didn't die.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Ahh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: That's all I did, honey, of course, I have been an instructor since. I've been flying for other people for a long time. All good, yeah.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: That's good.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: All good, yeah. And what else? I've never taken her for an airplane ride, have I?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: No, you haven't.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I'm still going to take care of that, okay.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Have you ever been for an airplane ride?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Airplane ride?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: You know what, you always want to give your guests a treat, right. There was a program, those who were young enough were drafted. We were supposed to go to Battle of the Bulge, and that was the last day in December of '44. Before I get on a boat, they found out I wasn't fit to qualify, so they didn't send me.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: They sent me back to Middletown here, the last place I served. See, I was in the peacetime army here in Middletown. Before 1939, before the war --

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, okay, yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I can't say war. -- anyhow, then they had found out I already was here so they sent me to another one for an engineer.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I'm retired from Middletown, and you know what, I got a letter from the Department of Aging, and if I make less than $11,500 a month, then they come and put my sewerage in for free.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, that's nice.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I make over that.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: That's not nice.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I'm not poor no more, and I don't know why they're so fussy about -- I got Meals On Wheels.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I pay $25 a month for that. They're pretty good but -- you got to go down to get the letters.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: When you were in the war, did you have anybody like write to you?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Write to me?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: My wife. She wrote to me the other day.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, well, did anybody else write to you?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Nobody else knew I was in the Army.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, okay. When we were in schools, we had to write to like soldiers that were in the war and stuff.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Oh, you can write to me.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I got a heck of a time reading and writing.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: No, I was home two or three times in that 19 months.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: You were stationed in Texas?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: You were in Texas?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I was in Texas once, yeah. I was in Texas just for a couple months. We were experimenting with spraying dust, spraying dust in an airplane.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I've done that before in my lifetime. I went down there and did it for Chanute. We had a good time. The first one I took one off, spark plugs come off. Every time it fires, you see the back it has got two plugs in them. You can see a plane go right back over you, and you duck.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: [ Laughter ]

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: That was a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Then where did you go after Texas, did you come back here?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: No, they put me in Georgia for a while. We were going to teach twin engines, they were going to send me to twin engine school, but, see, I never flown twin engines before I went in the service, I always flew Penn Harris. It only had one engine.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Then that fizzled because the war was close so they didn't need us anymore.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: They had an average of about four thousand pilots living in Cleveland. They were training girls to fly. I taught one class of girls.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I taught Betty Cobell, who lives behind me, I taught her to fly, I taught Holly Jillcote (sic) to fly from Harrisburg, I taught Grace Hoyt (sic) to fly from Harrisburg, I taught, what the hell's her name, I taught Sara Silcose (sic). Then weren't really -- they weren't gung ho enough to be in the Army.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, I see. Huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: They got to act smart, like you are.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, I see. A snob?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: A snob?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: More or less. When I was in Middletown, I was just an engineer here.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: That was the life.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Then you went from New Jersey to where?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Then you went to New Jersey, then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: No, I didn't go to New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: He went to Georgia.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, Georgia.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Macon, Georgia, where the peaches go.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Down south?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I never saw a Georgia peach though.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, you didn't?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: No, I saw some oranges but I didn't see a peach. I did all right though. I had a good time. I was in Florida a long time. As a matter of fact, one time I stay at my Brother's his house. I got paid $28 a day for my hotel room and $28 for my meals, and I asked if I could stay with my brother. We were working per diem.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, that's nice.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: That was pretty good.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: That was really good.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: But I had a good time except that my wife didn't like it.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: She was here, right?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: She was in Latrobe. That's the mistake I made. I took her home to my family, I should have taken her to her family.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: But I didn't know that they would have accepted her. She never knew her father, he died when she was two years old. Her mother had a husband. She should have went there. I should have taken her there.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: When you had kids and stuff, they were here though when you were out?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Well, for a while. She was in Latrobe, then she was in Royal Hannah, then they went to visit eastern Maryland where my sister lived. Her sister, two sisters lived there, and my wife had good time during the war, traveled all over the place, but when I got home from the service, she was in Royal Hannah.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Then because I was getting out of the service because I was injured, my legs were bad, they gave me a home in homestead, two homes there.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: And we moved down and we moved back, then I went to work, oh, all kinds of work. Boy, I did all kinds of work. When I left Middletown, I left on a bad note, and instead of giving me a hearing for my attitude, they went up and drafted me.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: And when I came back, I was looking for a job back here.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Two years and eight months I had to wait, then they gave me my job back. I went to work in Middletown in 1948, I was getting $1.10 an hour.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Man, can you imagine making that, 1.10 an hour?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I couldn't keep a family. My wife was working at Hart, they call it, sewing jackets.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: It's now a child center where they have all kinds of people living in there and all kinds of kids growing in there, retribution, you know what I mean?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Right, right. I know, yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Oh, half of those kids only had one parent, they only knew one parent, a guy came in living there for a while, he moved. You know what's downtown there, well, they used to make jackets there.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Now it's an apartment house for poor people. I'd move in there, but then it ain't for me. I'm going to find a place -- what's that place downtown?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Arts downtown.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Down in Hinesburg?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Hinesburg, yeah.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: They have a nice old age center. [ Tape turned off]

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: What did you do after you left there?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I left here legally, when did I leave here, April of '44, came back in December of '45.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: A little over two years?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Two years. When I left here, I lived in Nam before the war started, peacetime, I was in peacetime, I was in the CCC Corps.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: And when I left here to fly instruction, they were going to draft me. They couldn't draft me. All they had to do was call me.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: Then that made a fuss because I wanted my old rack back. They said no. I said yes. I went to call them up, the college, Dixon College, and taught some college tech. courses for the Army. I lived here then. I lived here in the old house around here, right off of here. There used to be a garage in the basement. Now they built it up.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: My kids and I and my wife and my sister-in-law lived in that house for four years. I tried to buy it so bad. I tried to buy it for your mother. She didn't like it.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: You can buy me a house, I'll like it.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I'm not in a position to buy a house. I have a couple of my banking accounts, I bank down here around the block.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: The First Union.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: I don't like them.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I have a checking account there. [ Tape turned off. ].

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: How many wars were you in?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I can't hear you.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: You have to talk louder. What was the question?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: How many wars were you in and what were they?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: You have to talk louder.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: How many wars --

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: You've got to say it louder.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Louder?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: You can say it so I can hear it.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: He wanted to know how many wars you were in?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: One. I didn't go to Korean War because I wasn't physically able, and Vietnam, I was way too old for Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: What war was that that you were in then?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: World War II, right?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: I was born in World War I. I was in World War II, I ain't going to World War III because there ain't going to be, it will be next door. We'll all be in it. One's enough. One's enough. They're stealing my money.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Who's stealing your money?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: The government does.

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: They beat me out of some, but they're going to give it to me. They're probably going to give it to my son after I die because he's heir to everything. What I don't understand -- [ Tape turned off. ].

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: How old were you when you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: How old were you when you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: How old was I, 1944, I must have been 24 years old, 24, 25. I was just a youngster. I didn't come in that 27-year bracket. If you were over 27, you wouldn't be drafted. See, I was drafted because I was in the peacetime Army in '38, '39. When I got discharged from the Army in '39, I went to work at Middletown as a civilian. I mean, $320 a month -- a year, a year. That was 1939. In 1940, I was a senior in Connecticut, $2200 a year, that was big time money, boy. My sister-in-law used to lived with us. You know Lena?

sp.speaker: Angelica Bouch
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Zito
sp.p: She worked for Hershey at the time, 40 cents an hour. [ Tape turned off. ].
